questions.prompt: “We’d never get the staff to learn a new system.” What is it?
questions.reveal: It’s a real concern you can answer.

questions.prompt: Right after your opener, before any conversation: “Just send me some info.” What is it, and what do you do?

options.text: A brush-off: earn attention with one relevant thing, then ask

questions.reveal: You haven’t earned attention yet. Sending info won’t change that.

questions.prompt: “Honestly, the owner handles all of that.” Best move?

options.text: It’s routing: find out who and when to reach them

questions.reveal: Change who you’re talking to, not what you’re saying.

questions.prompt: Why is the first no usually not the real answer?

options.text: A cold call is an interruption, so the first response is often a reflex

questions.reveal: “No thanks, just looking.” Half the time they did need help.

questions.prompt: What should you do before you choose a response?

options.text: Work out whether it’s a reflex, a real concern or a signal to stop

questions.reveal: Read it before you answer it.

questions.prompt: “Please take me off your list.” What now?

options.text: Stop, thank them and log it as do not call

questions.reveal: That’s a signal to stop, not an objection.

questions.prompt: When is the Ask step a question for more information, not the meeting?

options.text: When the objection was vague and you don’t know what’s behind it

questions.reveal: You can’t answer what you don’t understand yet.

questions.prompt: “It’s just not a fit for us.” Best next line?

options.text: “When you say it’s not a fit, what’s behind that?”

questions.reveal: Clarify before you answer.

questions.prompt: Which is the best isolating question?

options.text: “Is that the main thing, or is there something else that makes it a no?”

questions.reveal: It finds the real objection without putting them on the defensive.

questions.prompt: “I’ve migrated before. It was a nightmare.” Best response?

options.text: “Totally fair, and we’re getting a little ahead of ourselves. We hear that a lot, which is why we’ve put so much into a smooth onboarding. What made it so painful last time?”
“We have the best migration team around.”

questions.reveal: Disarm, name the onboarding focus without promising specifics, then clarify. The AE covers the details.

questions.prompt: What does “use the objection as the reason” mean?

options.text: Turning their concern into why the meeting is worth it

questions.reveal: “That’s exactly why it’s worth 15 minutes.”

questions.prompt: You clarified and they said “We tried an app before and clients never used it.” What next?

options.text: Tell them their clients were wrong
Acknowledge it, ask how clients book today, then tie it to the meeting

questions.reveal: Their real concern, answered with a question that keeps it moving.

questions.prompt: What’s the rule for a second objection?

options.text: A new objection gets a new acknowledge

questions.reveal: Repeating yourself tells them you weren’t listening.

questions.prompt: A Pilates owner says “It works fine,” you handle it, then: “We just don’t have the bandwidth to switch.” Best response?

options.text: “Totally get it. Switching is a lot. What’s eating most of the team’s time right now?”
“It only takes a day to switch.”

questions.reveal: Acknowledge the new one, then ask a question that can surface the pain.

questions.prompt: In a stack, where is the real objection usually?

options.text: Often the second, once the reflex is out of the way
Whatever they say right before hanging up

questions.reveal: The first is the reflex. The second is usually what’s really on their mind.

questions.prompt: “Bad timing,” then: “And honestly it’s probably too expensive anyway.” Best response?

options.text: “Fair enough. Price depends on the setup, and the AE covers that. What’s making this month so hectic?”

questions.reveal: No price, no argument, and back to the thread that matters.

questions.prompt: You’ve handled two objections and they’re still talking and asking questions. What now?

options.text: Ask for the meeting, tied to what they told you
Get ahead of a third objection

questions.reveal: They’re still in it. Go for the meeting.

questions.prompt: Which response to a second objection sounds most natural?

options.text: “Makes sense. Can I ask what’s behind that one?”

questions.reveal: It sounds like a person, and it clarifies.

questions.prompt: “We just switched to WellnessLiving last month.” Best response?

options.text: “What made you switch, and is there anything you wish it did?” Then log it honestly

questions.reveal: Respect the decision, learn something, log it.

questions.prompt: “We’re under contract.” Best first move?
questions.reveal: The answer tells you whether there’s a meeting to set now.

questions.prompt: “The owner picked our software.” Best response?

options.text: “Makes sense. Who would weigh in if you ever looked at options?”

questions.reveal: It’s routing in disguise.

questions.prompt: “Bad timing, we’re slammed.” Best response?

options.text: “No worries. What’s making it so busy right now?”

questions.reveal: Busy is often the pain.

questions.prompt: “Call me next quarter.” Best response?
questions.reveal: A real reason gets a real follow-up date. No reason means it was a brush-off.

questions.prompt: “We’re opening a new location in the spring, so not now.” Best response?

options.text: Treat it as a reason to meet: ask how they’re planning the new location’s schedule

questions.reveal: Growth is a reason to meet, not a reason to wait.

questions.prompt: When is an objection worth exploring?

options.text: They’re still talking and gave you a reason, not just a refusal

questions.reveal: A reason gives you something to work with.

questions.prompt: Where does an honestly logged “not interested” go?

options.text: Nurture, and it comes back as Recycled in three months

questions.reveal: A no you log honestly comes back to you.

questions.prompt: Where does a do-not-call request go?
questions.reveal: And it stays there.

questions.prompt: They’ve said no clearly twice, with no reason. What do you do?
questions.reveal: Persistence needs judgment.

questions.prompt: Why log a no honestly instead of arguing with it?

options.text: An honest no comes back later; an argued one is gone either way

questions.reveal: Arguing doesn’t save the lead.

questions.prompt: The prospect gives one-word answers and keeps saying they need to go. You’re the only one still in the conversation. What now?

options.text: Wrap up politely and log it honestly

questions.reveal: Time to stop.
